title: The marshmallow test
hook: The famous test of waiting for a second treat predicts less than people thought.
peek: Children who could wait alone with a marshmallow to earn a second one seemed to do better years later. A larger study in 2018 found the link was much weaker than the famous version, and shrank further once home life was taken into account.
lede: Around 1970, Walter Mischel offered preschoolers at Stanford's Bing Nursery School a choice: one treat now, or two if they could wait while the researcher left the room. Follow-ups years later found children who waited longer tended to have higher test scores. The story became a parenting legend. A bigger, more varied study in 2018 told a more modest tale.

bullets.text: The first long-term link came from a few dozen Bing children whose parents answered later surveys. They came from a single campus nursery, mostly from well-off university families, which limited how far the results could be stretched.

Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan used a national sample of about 900 children. The link between waiting and later achievement was around half the original size, and dropped by about two-thirds more once family background and early abilities were considered.

Mischel's films show children covering their eyes, singing, kicking the desk or turning away. He found that thinking of the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud, rather than as something sweet and chewy, helped them wait longer.

A 2013 study at the University of Rochester had an adult first break a small promise to some children. Those children waited far less than ones whose promise was kept, suggesting waiting is partly a sensible judgment about whether the reward will really come.
